analysis.title: GS Sector Specialists Energy, Natural Resources and Utilities Preview Conversations + Prints 2 Nov 2026
key_insights: FANG: GS specialists lean more cautious into the print, with a desk positioning score of 3/10. The four items investors want from the call are inorganic growth (Delaware vs Midland, bolt-on vs larger scale), capital allocation, efficiency gains plus Barnett, and gas strategy.
FANG capital allocation is in focus because the company doubled its share repurchase authorization last quarter, and the debate is return of capital vs growth vs leverage reduction with WTI at $98/b.

FANG gas strategy was called out more directly in the 2Q shareholder letter (LNG and data center opportunities). The company quote: 'We always talk internally that the Permian hasn't even tried to produce gas yet.'
The desk will also watch for commentary on cost inflation and capex potentially rising. Several Large Cap E&P prints this week will put this in focus for the group.

WMB: reports EPS after the close on 2 Nov with a call at 9:30 AM ET the next day. The desk positioning score is 9/10, and GS sees it as one of the most well owned equities in Midstream and in Energy broadly.

WMB trades in a $69-$75/sh band, with premarket indicating about $74/sh. Bulls see it as a low beta way to play the power theme, with behind-the-meter (BTM) execution and contracts trending the right way.

WMB's earnings driver is the base business (Transco). Last quarter the company raised its annual EBITDA growth target through 2030 to 11%+ from 10%+ and highlighted new gas transmission projects. GS says power is the 'cherry on the top'.

Market expectations are for at least one WMB BTM announcement before year-end, possibly two. It is debated whether it comes with EPS. A new customer for a larger scale project could drive a significant re-rate, and there are questions on customer mix and duration.
CCJ was the worst performer in GS's Energy/resources screen on Friday, when the whole group was under pressure, after FY production guidance was revised lower.
GS notes that a premier operator lowering production guidance has historically been a tailwind for the group, as a read that supply is tight, spot price support likely follows, and mining is hard.

GS found nothing negative on uranium on the CCJ call. Management said contract floors are in the mid-to-high-70s escalated, ceilings are touching $160 escalated, and the fixed base escalated portion is at three-digit uranium prices on very small volumes.

GS's illustrative midpoint of the contracting terms points to $115-$120/lb. Bears note floors and ceilings are unchanged from 2Q commentary, and GS responds that contracting moves higher over years in a stairstep.
GS argues that even if data center demand for nuclear fades, there is still underlying structural tightness on the supply side of uranium.
